children: Shares of credit reporting giant Equifax

jumped 6.3% in the afternoon session after Argus analyst John Eade upgraded the stock from Hold to Buy and set a $200 price target. According to TipRanks, Eade said Equifax has moved past its data-breach period onto a modest growth path, and that growth is starting to pick up as a new consumer credit-scoring model gains share. He also pointed to a recent double-digit dividend increase as a sign management is more confident in the cash-flow outlook. Argus said the shares trade at 17 times its 2027 earnings estimate, the low end of a historical range of 17 to 33 times. The upgrade follows a third quarter in which adjusted earnings of $2.26 a share beat the $2.20 consensus and revenue rose 9.6% to $1.69 billion, though mortgage-volume weakness and a fourth-quarter outlook below Street expectations remain the main pushback.
What is the market telling us

Equifax’s shares are somewhat volatile and have had 13 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 2 days ago when the stock gained 5.6% on the news that the company reported a 10% increase in third-quarter 2026 revenue to $1.693 billion, fueled by strong growth across its core business segments. According to a company press release, revenue rose 9% in local currency, propelled by an 8% gain in Diversified Markets and 13% growth in its U.S. Information Solutions (USIS) division. U.S. Mortgage revenue increased 15% despite challenging market conditions. Equifax also highlighted product innovation, noting that its new product Vitality Index—a measure of revenue generated from recent products—exceeded a record 17%. The company returned $158 million to shareholders through share repurchases and a quarterly dividend. This execution demonstrated solid operational momentum, offering investors confidence that growth in diversified data offerings could offset ongoing headwinds in the mortgage sector.

Equifax is down 12.6% since the beginning of the year, and at $187.04 per share, it is trading 20% below its 52-week high of $233.80 from October 2025. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Equifax’s shares 5 years ago would now be looking at only $697.18.
